title: Mohinder Panwar vs Afzal Ahmed on 10 March, 2014
full_text: Mohinder Panwar vs Afzal Ahmed on 10 March, 2014 IN THE COURT OF SHRI SANDEEP YADAV, ADDITIONAL SESSIONS JUDGE­5 (SOUTH), SAKET COURTS, NEW DELHI Appeal No.04/14 Mohinder Panwar s/o Late Shri Pyare Lal r/o H.No.5­1, Shahpur Jat, New Delhi­110049 ...... Appellant/Accused versus Afzal Ahmed Prop. M/s A.F. Interior Contractor s/o Shri Abdul Ghaffar r/o C­35, Tigri Extension, Khanpur, New Delhi ....... Respondent/Complainant Date of Institution : 21.09.2013 Final arguments heard on : 17.02.2014 Order pronounced on : 10.03.2014 ORDER 1. This appeal is directed against the judgment dated 26.08.2013 and the order on sentence dated 30.08.2013 passed by Shri Sunil Beniwal, ld. Metropolitan Magistrate­03, Metropolitan Magistrate (South). The appellant has been convicted u/s 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act vide judgment dated 26.08.2013 and has been sentenced to Rigorous Imprisonment for four months and has been further directed to pay compensation of Rs.50,000/­ to the respondent Mohinder Panwar vs. Afzal Ahmed Page No.1 Crl. Appeal No.04/14 vide order dated 30.08.2013. 2. The case set up by the respondent before the trial court is that the respondent is Painter by profession and is running his business under the name and style of M/s AF Interior Contractor. As per the avernment of the complaint, Appellant/accused, who was known to the respondent/complainant, gave a contract of painting and polishing to the respondent and the respondent finished the said work as per the specification and satisfaction of the appellant. The appellant made payment from time to time to the respondent and lastly a sum of Rs.1,75,000/­ was due from the appellant for the said job done by the respondent. Appellant in order to discharge of his part liability issued one post dated cheque bearing no.000005 dated 22.10.2011 for a sum of Rs.25,000/­ in favour of AF Interior Contractor with the assurance that the said cheque will be honored on its presentation. However when the respondent deposited the said cheque for encashment with its banker, same was returned unpaid with the remarks 'funds insufficient' vide return memo dated 23.12.2011. Immediately after receiving the information of dishonour of the cheque, the respondent informed the appellant about the same and demanded the cheque amount as well as balance in cash. However, the appellant failed to pay the amount in cash to the respondent. Left with no other alternative respondent got issued a legal notice dated 20.01.2012 under the Registered A.D. Cover. The said notice was duly Mohinder Panwar vs. Afzal Ahmed Page No.2 Crl. Appeal No.04/14 served on the appellant on 21.01.2012. However despite the service of legal notice the appellant did not pay the cheque amount to the respondent. The respondent then prayed in the complaint that appellant be summoned, tried and prosecuted for the offence u/s 138 / 117 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. 3. The respondent led pre­summoning evidence and thereafter the appellant was summoned. Accusation u/s 251 Cr.PC was explained to the appellant. Appellant pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. Thereafter the respondent led evidence and filed his evidence by way of affidavit and proved the legal notice as Ex.CW1/C, postal receipt as Ex.CW1/D, dishonored cheque was proved as Ex.CW1/A and the cheque returning memo was proved as Ex.CW1/B. Respondent also examined the witness from the bank. Statement of the appellant u/s 313 Cr.PC was recorded and the appellant denied all the incriminating evidence against him. Appellant examined himself as DW1 and proved the photocopy of his Election Voter Identity Card, Arm Licence, photocopy of Driving licence and passport which were exhibited as Ex.DW1/1 (colly). Originals of all these documents were shown to the court and were returned. 4. I have heard ld. Counsel for the appellant at length and carefully perused the Trial court recored. The main thrust of the appellant in the appeal is that legal notice as mandated u/s 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act was not served on the appellant. The Mohinder Panwar vs. Afzal Ahmed Page No.3 Crl. Appeal No.04/14 impugned judgment was assailed by the appellant on the ground that various documents produced by the appellant showing his address as H.No.5­I, Shahpur Jat, New Delhi was not considered by the Trial court. It is further contended in the appeal that demand notice has not been sent on the correct address of the appellant and hence same was not delivered to the appellant. It is also stated in the appeal that trial court failed to consider the fact that even the complaint filed by the respondent does not bear the correct address of the appellant and for this reason the envelope containing the summons of the case was received back undelivered. Appellant states that just two days after the receipt of the same through his wife, appellant appeared before the trial court and offered to pay the cheque amount but the respondent was not present in the court and his counsel was not aware about the whereabout of the respondent and hence the matter was adjourned. 5. Service of the notice in writing on the drawer by the drawee demanding the payment of cheque amount is vital ingredient of Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act. If the said ingredient is not proved by the complainant, the drawer of the cheque cannot be convicted u/s 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act. 6. In 2010 (1) DCR 658 Delhi High Court in HDFC Bank Limited vs. Amit Kumar Singh , the requirement of serving the legal notice upon the drawer of the cheque was discussed in detail by the Hon'ble High Court and it was held as under:­ Mohinder Panwar vs. Afzal Ahmed Page No.4 Crl. Appeal No.04/14 "This Court is unable to accept the proposition that by merely filing an affidavit stating that the drawer resides at the address given in the legal notice, the complainant can satisfy the requirement of having to satisfy the Court that notice was in fact was delivered to the drawer. In the considered view of this Court, such an affidavit can be accepted only if the deponent states that he either went personally and found that the accused was residing at the address or is able to produce some postal certificate or an endorsement by a courier service agency that the accused is infact residing at the address and yet refusing to accept the notice. If the affidavit merely states that the accused is residing at the address without giving any further documentary proof in support thereof such an affidavit cannot be accepted as satisfying the requirement of Section138(b) read with Section 138(c) of the NI Act. 7. In the present case the affidavit filed by the respondent does not even show that the accused is residing at the address mentioned in the legal notice. The affidavit filed by the respondent merely states that the respondent got issued legal demand notice dated 20.01.2012 under the Registered AD Cover and the said notice was duly served on the appellant. It is nowhere deposed in the said affidavit that the respondent/complainant went personally and found that the appellant/accused was residing at the address mentioned in the legal notice nor has the respondent proved some postal receipts or the endorsement by the courier agency that the appellant is not found Mohinder Panwar vs. Afzal Ahmed Page No.5 Crl. Appeal No.04/14 residing at the address mentioned in the legal notice. The postal envelope through which the legal notice was sent has not been placed on record by the respondent. In the body of the legal notice the address of the appellant has been mentioned as, "Mohinder Panwar s/o Not Known, r/o 1/5, Shahpur Jat, Hauz Khas, New Delhi". However in the complaint, the address of the appellant is mentioned as " Mohinder Panwar s/o Not Known r/o B­1/15, Shahpur Jat, Hauz Khas, New Delhi". It is no where stated in the complaint or in the affidavit that after the service of the legal notice the appellant has changed his address. In fact the respondent in cross examination deposed that the legal notice Ex.CW1/C was sent at the address B­1/5, Shahpur Jat, Hauz Khas, New Delhi and not at B­1/15. Respondent/complainant further deposed in cross examination that he cannot say whether there is any house situated at House no.B­1/15, Shahpur Jat, Hauz Khas, New Delhi. Respondent/complainant further deposed that he cannot say that whether the address of the accused is i (I)5 and not B­1/5. Respondent further deposed that appellant might not have received the notice Ex.CW1/C. Therefore, no cogent evidence was led by the respondent to prove that the legal notice Ex.CW1/C was served at the correct address of the appellant. Hence one of the essential ingredient of the section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act viz. Service of the legal notice was not proved in the present case. 8. The trial court while addressing this issue relied upon the CC Mohinder Panwar vs. Afzal Ahmed Page No.6 Crl. Appeal No.04/14 Alvi Haji vs Palapetty Muhammed and anr. decided by Hon'ble Supreme Court on 18.05.2007. The trial court observed that the intention of the Hon'ble Supreme Court was to interpret this provision of mandatory legal notice in a harmonious way with all the objects and reason in enacting the statute of Negotiable instruments Act. The trial court observed that by no stretch of imagination it could be construed that if the mandatory notice under section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act was not served upon the drawer, then he could go scot free from his liability to pay the cheque amount. Trial court held that the accused cannot be granted this interpretation which defeats the very purpose of object of enacting the Negotiable Instruments Act and the stringent provisions therein for dishonour of a cheque issued by the drawer. These observations were made by the trial court in ignorance of the law laid down by Hon'ble Supreme Court in Harman Electronics (P) Ltd. vs. National Panasonic 2008 (16) SCALE 317. In this case Hon'ble Supreme Court emphasized the importance of service of notice on the drawer as contrasted with mere dispatch of the notice. In para 14 it was held as under:­ " It is one thing to say that sending of a notice is one of the ingredients for maintaining the complaint but it is another thing to say that dishonour of a cheque by itself constitutes an offence. For the purpose of proving its case that the accused had committed an offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, the ingredients thereof are required to be proved. What Mohinder Panwar vs. Afzal Ahmed Page No.7 Crl. Appeal No.04/14 would constitute an offence is stated in the main provision. The proviso appended thereto, however, imposes certain further conditions which are required to be fulfilled before cognizance of the offence can be taken. If the ingredients for constitution of the offence laid down in the provisos (a), (b) and (c) appended to Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act intended to be applied in favour of the accused, there cannot be any doubt that receipt of a notice would ultimately give rise to the cause of action for filing a complaint. As it is only on receipt of the notice the accused at his own peril may refuse to pay the amount. Clauses (b) and (c) of the proviso to Section 138 therefore must be read together. Issuance of notice would not by itself give rise to a cause of action but communication of the notice would." 9. In another judgment Dalmia Cement (Bharat) Ltd. vs. Galaxy Traders and Agencies Ltd. (2001) 6 Supreme Court cases 463 it was held that, " for constitution of an offence under Section 138 of the Act, notice must be received by the accused". In the present case the complainant has miserably failed to prove that the legal notice sent by the complainant has been received by the accused/appellant. 10. In CC Alvi Haji (Supra) it was held in para 17 as under:­ "It is also to be borne in mind that the requirement of giving of notice is a clear departure from the rule of Criminal Law, where there is no stipulation of giving of a notice before filing a complaint. Any drawer who claims that he did not receive the notice sent by post, can, within 15 days of receipt of Mohinder Panwar vs. Afzal Ahmed Page No.8 Crl. Appeal No.04/14 summons from the court in respect of the complaint under Section 138 of the Act, make payment of the cheque amount and submit to the Court that he had made payment within 15 days of receipt of summons (by receiving a copy of complaint with the summons) and, therefore, the complaint is liable to be rejected. A person who does not pay within 15 days of receipt of the summons from the Court along with the coy of the complaint under Section 138 of the Act, cannot obviously contend that there was no proper service of notice as required under Section 138 , by ignoring statutory presumption to the contrary under Section 27 of the G.C. Act and Section 114 of the Evidence Act. In our view, any other interpretation of the proviso would defeat the very object of the legislation. As observed in Bhaskaran case(supra), if the giving of notice in the context of Clause (b) of the proviso was the same as the receipt of notice a trickster cheque drawer would get the premium to avoid receiving the notice by adopting different strategies and escape from legal consequences of Section 138 of the Act." 11. Appellant after being served with the summons appeared before the court on 19.12.2012 and offered to pay the cheque amount to the respondent. However since on that day none was present on behalf of the respondent and even the counsel for the respondent was not aware about the whereabout of the respondent the matter was adjourned for payment of cheque amount to 21.02.2013. On the next date i.e. on 21.02.2013 ld. Presiding officer was on leave and the ld. Counsel for Mohinder Panwar vs. Afzal Ahmed Page No.9 Crl. Appeal No.04/14 the appellant again submitted that appellant was ready to pay the cheque amount but the same was not accepted by the respondent. On the next date ie. on 09.05.2013 when ld. Counsel for the appellant submitted that the appellant had tendered cheque amount and wanted to settle the matter, the respondent submitted that his real claim was for Rs.1.5lacs and he is not ready to settle the matter for Rs.25,000/­. Therefore, it is clear from the record of this case that appellant from the first date of hearing was willing and ready to pay the cheque amount to the respondent but the respondent was not accepting the cheque amount. The appellant cannot be expected to forcibly put the cheque amount in the pocket of the respondent. In other words the appellant has complied with the mandate of law laid down in Hazi Ali case. 12. Since one of the essential ingredient of Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act i.e. the service of the legal notice upon the appellant was not proved in this case it cannot be concluded that accused has committed an offence u/s 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act . Accordingly the appeal succeeds and the appellant is acquitted. The judgment dated 26.08.2013 and the order on sentence dated 30.08.2013 are set aside. Bail bonds of accused are cancelled. Surety stands discharged. Trial court record be sent back with the copy of this order. Appeal file be consigned to record room. Announced in the open court ( Sandeep Yadav ) on 10.03.2014 Addl. Sessions Judge ­5 (South ) Saket Courts, New Delhi Mohinder Panwar vs. Afzal Ahmed Page No.10 Crl. Appeal No.04/14
